question.:question/problem:
![](images/fb/fbbb7c260754e6579bedc6e773656ea8defdb0493117f05e0e5f02fab4afb36c.png)

Evaluate the surface integral

$$\iint_S 1\,\mathrm{d}S,$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=- x + y$ and whose domain is the disk of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above. Give an exact answer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x + y)=-1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x + y)=1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{1}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(1)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(1)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{1}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 1,\ 0\le\theta\le 2 \pi\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{1}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(1)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\int_{0}^{1}{r}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[\frac{r^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\left[((\frac{1}{2}))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{2 \pi}{\frac{1}{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})\left[\theta\right]_{0}^{2 \pi} \\ & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})\left[((2 \pi))-((0))\right] \\ & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})\cdot((2 \pi)-(0)) \\ & =\sqrt{3} \pi.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $\sqrt{3} \pi$.

question.:question/problem:
![](images/79/79b09a881e6809e097e982b58d81a037d162f6b5820894e172955df1551415ca.png)

Evaluate the surface integral

$$\iint_S x\,\mathrm{d}S,$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=- x + y$ and whose domain is the right half-circle of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above. Give an exact answer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x + y)=-1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x + y)=1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{x}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(x)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(x)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{x}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 1,\ - \frac{\pi}{2}\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{x}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{((r\cos\theta))\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{r^{2} \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\int_{0}^{1}{r^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\left[\frac{r^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\cos{\left(\theta \right)})\left[((\frac{1}{3}))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{\frac{\cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})\left[\sin{\left(\theta \right)}\right]_{- \frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})\left[((1))-((-1))\right] \\ & =(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3})\cdot((1)-(-1)) \\ & =\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $\frac{2 \sqrt{3}}{3}$.

For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x - y)=1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(x - y)=-1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{y}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(y)\cdot\sqrt{1+(1)^2+(-1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(y)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{y}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 2,\ 0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{y}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{((r\sin\theta))\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\int_{0}^{2}{r^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\left[\frac{r^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\left[((\frac{8}{3}))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{\frac{8 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3})\left[- \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =(\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3})\left[((0))-((-1))\right] \\ & =(\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3})\cdot((0)-(-1)) \\ & =\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $\frac{8 \sqrt{3}}{3}$.

Evaluate the surface integral

$$\iint_S 4 y\,\mathrm{d}S,$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=- x - y$ and whose domain is the quarter-circle in the first quadrant of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above. Give an exact answer.
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,\mathrm{d}S=\iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}\,\mathrm{d}A.$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(- x - y)=-1,$$

and

$$\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(- x - y)=-1.$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_S{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}S & =\iint_D{f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4 y)\cdot\sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(-1)^2}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =\iint_D{(4 y)\cdot\sqrt{3}}\,\mathrm{d}A \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

$$\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\le r\le 1,\ 0\le\theta\le \frac{\pi}{2}\}.$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\sqrt{3})\iint_D{4 y}\,\mathrm{d}A & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{(4(r\sin\theta))\cdot r}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\iint_\Delta{4 r^{2} \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\int_{0}^{1}{4 r^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}r}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\left[\frac{4 r^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{(\sin{\left(\theta \right)})\left[((\frac{4}{3}))-((0))\right]}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\sqrt{3})\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}{\frac{4 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{3}}\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ & =(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3})\left[- \cos{\left(\theta \right)}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ & =(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3})\left[((0))-((-1))\right] \\ & =(\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3})\cdot((0)-(-1)) \\ & =\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral is $\frac{4 \sqrt{3}}{3}$.
